canonical_statement: The review objective was to determine the effect of Ashwagandha extract on sleep in adults.
The review protocol was prospectively registered in PROSPERO as CRD42021229064 and the meta-analysis was conducted according to PRISMA.
At PROSPERO registration, preliminary searches had started, while formal screening, data extraction, risk-of-bias assessment, and data analysis had not started.

Eligible studies were randomized controlled trials in adults older than 18 years, with or without insomnia, using Ashwagandha extract in any form, dose, or duration and evaluating at least one sleep outcome.

population.label: Adults >18 years with or without insomnia

canonical_statement: The published review included placebo-controlled randomized trials; the registered protocol allowed placebo or no-treatment comparators.

exposures.details: Protocol comparator: placebo or no treatment; published trials used placebo

canonical_statement: The primary review outcome was sleep quantity and sleep quality, including subjective scales and actigraphy-derived sleep parameters.

outcome.definition: Sleep assessed with sleep scales, PSQI, sleep-efficiency measures, sleep logs, actigraphy, or polysomnography as available
outcome.measurement_method: Subjective sleep scales and objective sleep measures

canonical_statement: Secondary outcomes were mental alertness on rising, anxiety level, quality of life, and safety/adverse events.

outcome.definition: Mental alertness on rising, anxiety, quality of life, and adverse events

canonical_statement: The investigators searched CENTRAL, MEDLINE, SCOPUS, Google Scholar, WHO trials, ClinicalTrials.gov, CTRI, Google, and AYUSH resources through February 2021, hand-searched references, and contacted manufacturers for unpublished trials.
The review limited inclusion to English-language studies but imposed no publication-date restriction.
The supporting search-strategy file documents explicit CENTRAL and MEDLINE terms combining Ashwagandha synonyms with sleep, insomnia, and quality-of-life terms.
Two authors independently screened and extracted data, disagreements were resolved with a third author, and intention-to-treat data were used when study reports allowed.
Risk of bias was assessed across random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting, and other bias using Cochrane Handbook domains.

Meta-analyses used Review Manager 5.4 with random-effects pooling; continuous outcomes used mean difference or standardized mean difference with 95% confidence intervals, dichotomous outcomes were planned as risk ratios, and heterogeneity was assessed with I-squared.
GRADE was used to rate certainty for primary and secondary outcomes across risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias.

Planned subgroup analyses included sleep-measure type, age, insomnia status, extract form, dose, and treatment duration; the published review could analyze only measure type, insomnia status, dose, and duration because of insufficient data.

The search returned 1,236 database records plus four records from other sources; 1,094 records remained after deduplication, 10 full texts were assessed, and five randomized trials met inclusion criteria.
The review included five randomized placebo-controlled trials with 400 unique participants; all trials were conducted in India.

population.label: Participants across five included RCTs conducted in India

canonical_statement: The included evidence comprised 210 healthy adults across two trials, 50 healthy adults aged over 60 years in one trial, 60 adults with DSM-IV insomnia in one trial, and one 80-person trial containing 40 healthy adults and 40 adults with DSM-IV insomnia.

population.label: Five included RCTs: healthy, elderly, and insomnia populations

canonical_statement: All five trials used oral Ashwagandha capsules: four used KSM-66 root extract and one used Shoden root-and-leaf extract; daily doses ranged from 120 mg to 600 mg and study durations from 6 to 12 weeks.

exposures.details: Across trials: KSM-66 root extract in four RCTs; Shoden root-and-leaf extract in one RCT; 120-600 mg/day; 6-12 weeks

canonical_statement: All five trials reported no serious adverse effects; one trial reported mild events in the Ashwagandha group including viral fever, headache, acid reflux, and allergic dermatitis.

All five trials described computer-generated randomization; one trial had unclear allocation concealment and unclear blinding details, one trial was judged high risk for incomplete outcome data, and only two trials were prospectively registered.
The review reported a significant improvement in overall sleep with Ashwagandha versus placebo (SMD -0.59, 95% CI -0.75 to -0.42; I²=62%; p<0.001; moderate-certainty evidence).

canonical_statement: Sensitivity analyses excluding or accounting for trials with unclear sequence-generation or allocation-concealment risk did not materially change effect sizes or confidence intervals.
Only five trials with 400 unique participants were included, and only one trial enrolled older adults; the authors cautioned that applicability to elderly populations was limited.
The review excluded non-English-language studies and could not be certain that all unpublished trials were identified; too few studies were available for funnel-plot assessment of publication bias.

Sleep outcomes were measured with heterogeneous tools; actigraphy estimates sleep from movement rather than directly measuring sleep, and the seven-point Sleep Quality Scale was uncommon, inconsistent across trials, and based on small samples.
The authors identified substantial heterogeneity for multiple sleep outcomes and serious imprecision for most primary outcomes because included trials were small.
The included trials averaged about eight weeks in duration, leaving limited evidence on long-term efficacy and serious adverse effects.

The authors concluded that Ashwagandha extract appears to improve subjective and objective sleep in adults, with apparently larger effects at doses of at least 600 mg/day and durations of at least 8 weeks, while emphasizing limited serious-adverse-effect and long-term safety data.
